title: What Do Earthworms Like? A Parent Guide
endLine: Earthworms breathe through moist skin, so most choose damp, dark places.

scenes.tts: Where do earthworms go on a hot, dry day? After rain, you may find them under a log. With a baking tray, you and your child can see which conditions the worms move toward.
scenes.caption: Where do earthworms go on a hot, dry day? After rain, you may find them under a log. With a baking tray, you and your child can see which conditions the worms move toward.
scenes.visual: Open on the same log in two schematic views, one after rain and one on a hot, dry day. Put the opening question on screen. Show an adult using a stick to tilt the log toward themselves in the rain view. Reveal a few worms on the damp soil and label the paired views “After rain” and “Hot, dry day”. Transition to the baking tray.
scenes.narration: Where do earthworms go on a hot, dry day? After rain, you may find them under a log. With a baking tray, you and your child can see which conditions the worms move toward.

scenes.visual: Title card over the clean schematic tabletop view of the empty baking tray with two soft-illustrated earthworms curving across the border. High-contrast large title text 'What Do Earthworms Like?' settles cleanly for two seconds while subtle ambient water-shimmer lines drift across the corner.

scenes.tts: Allow about thirty-five minutes once you have your worms. Your child practices looking closely, making a prediction, and checking it. You’ll change one thing at a time, count where the worms go, and repeat the test.
scenes.caption: Allow about thirty-five minutes once you have your worms. Your child practices looking closely, making a prediction, and checking it. You’ll change one thing at a time, count where the worms go, and repeat the test.
scenes.visual: Show paper towels, plain water, a cardboard cover, a timer and a tally sheet around the baking tray. Animate a worm crossing the center line, then show the tray covered. When the schematic timer reaches ten minutes, lift the cover and show a tally mark for the side where the worm is now.
scenes.narration: Allow about thirty-five minutes once you have your worms. Your child practices looking closely, making a prediction, and checking it. You’ll change one thing at a time, count where the worms go, and repeat the test.

scenes.tts: Start with six to ten earthworms from a bait shop or a damp garden bed. Stay with your child throughout. You do the digging. Keep the worms in damp soil in the shade and use them that day.
scenes.caption: Start with six to ten earthworms from a bait shop or a damp garden bed. Stay with your child throughout. You do the digging. Keep the worms in damp soil in the shade and use them that day.
scenes.visual: Show a bait tub and a damp garden bed as alternatives. At the garden bed, show an adult working the trowel while the child watches. Move the collected worms into a shaded container with damp soil.
scenes.narration: Start with six to ten earthworms from a bait shop or a damp garden bed. Stay with your child throughout. You do the digging. Keep the worms in damp soil in the shade and use them that day.

scenes.tts: Have children stand back about six feet. Tilt the log or rock toward you with a stick so it shields you. Never touch snakes or animals that bite or sting. Never taste outdoor plants, berries, or mushrooms.
scenes.caption: Have children stand back about six feet. Tilt the log or rock toward you with a stick so it shields you. Never touch snakes or animals that bite or sting. Never taste outdoor plants, berries, or mushrooms.
scenes.visual: Use the same garden view. Show the adult and stick tilting a log toward the adult, with the log between the adult and the ground underneath. Mark the child’s distance with a line labeled “About six feet”. Then show separate crossed-out icons for touching a snake and tasting a berry.
scenes.narration: Have children stand back about six feet. Tilt the log or rock toward you with a stick so it shields you. Never touch snakes or animals that bite or sting. Never taste outdoor plants, berries, or mushrooms.

scenes.tts: A thrashing worm with a smooth, milky-white band may be a jumping worm. Leave it and its soil there. Take a photo and ask your local Extension office.
scenes.caption: A thrashing worm with a smooth, milky-white band may be a jumping worm. Leave it and its soil there. Take a photo and ask your local Extension office.
scenes.visual: Show a schematic close-up of a worm with a smooth, pale band thrashing on the ground. Show the adult taking a photo, with the worm and soil staying in place.
scenes.narration: A thrashing worm with a smooth, milky-white band may be a jumping worm. Leave it and its soil there. Take a photo and ask your local Extension office.

scenes.tts: Keep worms, bits of soil, pebbles, and plastic wrap away from children under four. Call nine one one if someone is choking.
scenes.caption: Keep worms, bits of soil, pebbles, and plastic wrap away from children under four. Call nine one one if someone is choking.
scenes.visual: Show the four items on the adult’s side of the worktable. Put “Keep away from children under 4” beside the items, then change the label to “Call 911 if choking”.
scenes.narration: Keep worms, bits of soil, pebbles, and plastic wrap away from children under four. Call nine one one if someone is choking.

scenes.tts: Wet your hands and your child’s. Never squeeze or drop a worm. Watch one on a damp paper towel for a minute or two. Ask, "Which end is the front?" The band is near the front. You may hear bristles scratch.
scenes.caption: Wet your hands and your child’s. Never squeeze or drop a worm. Watch one on a damp paper towel for a minute or two. Ask, "Which end is the front?" The band is near the front. You may hear bristles scratch.
scenes.visual: On the same worktable, show wet hands gently moving a worm onto a damp paper towel. Zoom into the band near the front and show a schematic close-up of the tiny bristles gripping the paper.
scenes.narration: Wet your hands and your child’s. Never squeeze or drop a worm. Watch one on a damp paper towel for a minute or two. Ask, "Which end is the front?" The band is near the front. You may hear bristles scratch.

scenes.tts: Line the tray with paper towels. Keep one half dry. Dampen the other with plain water, stopping before puddles form. Ask, "Which side will the worms go to, damp or dry?"
scenes.caption: Line the tray with paper towels. Keep one half dry. Dampen the other with plain water, stopping before puddles form. Ask, "Which side will the worms go to, damp or dry?"
scenes.visual: Show the tray from above. Animate the paper towels lining the tray, a little plain water dampening one half, and the adult pointing to both sides. Label the halves “Damp” and “Dry”.
scenes.narration: Line the tray with paper towels. Keep one half dry. Dampen the other with plain water, stopping before puddles form. Ask, "Which side will the worms go to, damp or dry?"

scenes.tts: Place the worms across the middle line. Cover the whole tray with cardboard so both sides are equally dark. After ten minutes, count each side. Count any worm on the line as middle.
scenes.caption: Place the worms across the middle line. Cover the whole tray with cardboard so both sides are equally dark. After ten minutes, count each side. Count any worm on the line as middle.
scenes.visual: Place the schematic worms along the center line, slide the cardboard over the entire tray, and show a schematic timer advancing to ten minutes. Lift the cover and point to the tally columns for damp, dry and middle.
scenes.narration: Place the worms across the middle line. Cover the whole tray with cardboard so both sides are equally dark. After ten minutes, count each side. Count any worm on the line as middle.

scenes.tts: Suppose six of eight worms end up on the damp left side. Imagine turning the tray so the damp half is on the right. Where do you predict most worms will end up this time?
scenes.caption: Suppose six of eight worms end up on the damp left side. Imagine turning the tray so the damp half is on the right. Where do you predict most worms will end up this time?
scenes.visual: Reveal a schematic example using the eight worms from the guide’s figure. Show six on damp, one on dry and one in the middle. Before turning the tray, add the question “Where will most worms go after the swap?”
scenes.narration: Suppose six of eight worms end up on the damp left side. Imagine turning the tray so the damp half is on the right. Where do you predict most worms will end up this time?

scenes.visual: Hold the same tray view and the question “Where will most worms go after the swap?” for the silent thinking pause. Keep the worms moving subtly.

scenes.tts: Turn the tray around. Ask, "Do you think more worms will end up on the damp side again?" Return the worms to the middle and cover the tray. After ten minutes, count again. Add the damp counts together, then the dry counts.
scenes.caption: Turn the tray around. Ask, "Do you think more worms will end up on the damp side again?" Return the worms to the middle and cover the tray. After ten minutes, count again. Add the damp counts together, then the dry counts.
scenes.visual: Rotate the same tray so damp is on the right. Move the worms to the line and replace the cardboard. Advance a schematic timer, then lift the cover. Show which tally columns to add across the two runs without filling in a second-trial result.
scenes.narration: Turn the tray around. Ask, "Do you think more worms will end up on the damp side again?" Return the worms to the middle and cover the tray. After ten minutes, count again. Add the damp counts together, then the dry counts.

scenes.tts: Earthworms breathe through their skin, which has to stay moist. Most move away from dry ground and bright light toward damp, dark places.
scenes.caption: Earthworms breathe through their skin, which has to stay moist. Most move away from dry ground and bright light toward damp, dark places.
scenes.visual: Transform the tray into a schematic close-up of a worm on moist soil. Show oxygen dots passing through its moist skin while the worm moves beneath the surface.
scenes.narration: Earthworms breathe through their skin, which has to stay moist. Most move away from dry ground and bright light toward damp, dark places.

scenes.tts: For the optional light test, dampen the tray evenly. Keep it out of direct sun. Cover half with cardboard and half with a clear lid. Use bright room light. Or set a cool LED lamp about two feet above the clear half, away from water.
scenes.caption: For the optional light test, dampen the tray evenly. Keep it out of direct sun. Cover half with cardboard and half with a clear lid. Use bright room light. Or set a cool LED lamp about two feet above the clear half, away from water.
scenes.visual: Dampen both halves of the same tray. Show cardboard and a clear lid side by side before lowering them over the halves. Show bright room light falling on the clear half. Then show the optional setup with an adult placing a cool LED lamp about two feet above the clear half, with the lamp and cord away from the water cup.
scenes.narration: For the optional light test, dampen the tray evenly. Keep it out of direct sun. Cover half with cardboard and half with a clear lid. Use bright room light. Or set a cool LED lamp about two feet above the clear half, away from water.

scenes.tts: Earthworms have no eyes. Their skin senses light. Predict where they’ll go. Start them in the middle. Cover both halves to keep them equally damp. Count after ten minutes. Swap covers, move the lamp if used, and repeat.
scenes.caption: Earthworms have no eyes. Their skin senses light. Predict where they’ll go. Start them in the middle. Cover both halves to keep them equally damp. Count after ten minutes. Swap covers, move the lamp if used, and repeat.
scenes.visual: Move the worms to the center before lowering both covers. Use the same schematic timer, lift the covers, and show the tally sheet. Swap the cardboard and lid. In the lamp setup, show the adult shifting the lamp to the clear side. Reset the timer.
scenes.narration: Earthworms have no eyes. Their skin senses light. Predict where they’ll go. Start them in the middle. Cover both halves to keep them equally damp. Count after ten minutes. Swap covers, move the lamp if used, and repeat.

scenes.tts: Mist yard worms with plain water. Return them to damp soil in the shade where you found them. Watch them burrow. Never release bait-shop worms outdoors. Wash your hands with soap and water.
scenes.caption: Mist yard worms with plain water. Return them to damp soil in the shade where you found them. Watch them burrow. Never release bait-shop worms outdoors. Wash your hands with soap and water.
scenes.visual: Show the adult returning yard worms to the same shady patch and the child watching them burrow. Show a separate bait tub with a “Never release outside” label and finish on a handwashing icon before the end card.
scenes.narration: Mist yard worms with plain water. Return them to damp soil in the shade where you found them. Watch them burrow. Never release bait-shop worms outdoors. Wash your hands with soap and water.

scenes.line: Earthworms breathe through moist skin, so most choose damp, dark places.
scenes.visual: Clean high-contrast end card over the calm dark-soil cross-section with gentle underground earthworm tunnels slowly glowing. Centered large text displays the exact take-home line: 'Earthworms breathe through moist skin, so most choose damp, dark places.'
